concept.name: Trade expectancy
concept.definition: The average amount a trading system can be expected to make or lose per trade: the probability-weighted mean of trade outcomes, win rate times average winner minus loss rate times average loser. In Van Tharp's framework it is expressed as the mean R-multiple — expected profit per dollar of initial risk.
concept.intuition: It is the single number that says whether a system has an edge: how much, on average, each trade adds to or subtracts from the account.
concept.mechanics: From a closed-trade sample compute the win rate, average win, and average loss and combine them; equivalently, take the mean of all trade PnLs or R-multiples. Multiply by trade frequency (opportunity) for expected profit per period; position sizing then converts expectancy into actual returns.
concept.formula: E = p * avgWin - (1 - p) * avgLoss; in R terms, E[R] = (1/N) * sum_i R_i, where R_i is trade i's PnL divided by its initial risk.
concept.failure_modes: Expectancy estimated from few trades is dominated by sampling error, and backtested expectancy rarely survives costs, slippage, and regime change. It is a mean: it hides variance and tail risk, so a positive-expectancy system can still be ruined by reckless sizing.
concept.misconceptions: Positive expectancy does not mean every sequence of trades profits, and expectancy is not a fixed property of the rules — the same system in a different regime produces a different expectancy. Position sizing cannot rescue a negative-expectancy system.
concept.example: A system that wins 40% of trades with 3R average winners and 1R average losers has expectancy 0.4 * 3 - 0.6 * 1 = +0.6R per trade.
